description: A two-panel tensile-property figure for as-cast Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr (x = 0, 3, 6, 9) strips. (a) Engineering stress (MPa, y-axis 0–1000) versus engineering strain (%, x-axis 0–50), with four curves keyed by the legend entries "0Cr" (solid black), "3Cr" (red dashed), "6Cr" (blue dotted) and "9Cr" (teal dash-dot). The 0Cr curve yields near 700 MPa and extends furthest, to roughly 48% strain; the Cr-bearing curves terminate earlier — 3Cr near 40%, and 6Cr and 9Cr near 22–26% — while 6Cr and 9Cr rise to the highest stress level, close to the 1000 MPa top gridline, with a small load drop before final fracture. (b) plots true stress (MPa, left axis 0–1500) and strain hardening rate (MPa, right axis 1000–4000) against true strain (0–0.4) for the same four alloys and the same legend. True-stress curves rise monotonically with strain, whereas the strain-hardening-rate curves fall steeply from an initial peak and settle onto a plateau that is lowest for 0Cr and rises progressively with Cr content. The figure argues that Cr addition raises ultimate tensile strength and steady-stage strain-hardening rate while reducing total elongation.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress (MPa, 0–1000) vs engineering strain (%, 0–50) for four as-cast alloys: 0Cr (solid black), 3Cr (red dashed), 6Cr (blue dotted), 9Cr (teal dash-dot). 0Cr reaches the largest strain (~48%), 3Cr ends near 40%, while 6Cr and 9Cr end near 22–26% but attain the highest stress, approaching 1000 MPa.

Dual-axis plot of true stress (MPa, left, 0–1500) and strain hardening rate (MPa, right, 1000–4000) vs true strain (0–0.4) for 0Cr, 3Cr, 6Cr and 9Cr. True stress increases monotonically; strain hardening rate drops steeply from an initial high value and forms a plateau that increases in level from 0Cr through 3Cr, 6Cr to 9Cr.

observations.observation: Panel (a) is an engineering stress-strain plot with y-axis 'Engineering stress (MPa)' spanning 0 to 1000 and x-axis 'Engineering strain (%)' spanning 0 to 50.
Both panels carry the identical legend labels '0Cr' (solid black), '3Cr' (red dashed), '6Cr' (blue dotted) and '9Cr' (teal dash-dot).
In (a), the 0Cr curve reaches the largest engineering strain (near the 48–50% end of the axis), whereas the 6Cr and 9Cr curves terminate at roughly 22–26% strain.
In (a), the 6Cr and 9Cr curves attain the highest engineering stress, approaching the 1000 MPa top gridline, and both show a small load drop shortly before final fracture.
Panel (b) uses two y-axes: left 'True stress (MPa)' from 0 to 1500, right 'Strain hardening rate (MPa)' from 1000 to 4000, with x-axis 'True strain' from 0.0 to 0.4.

In (b) the true-stress curves rise monotonically with true strain for all four alloys, while the strain hardening rate curves drop steeply from an initial peak and then plateau before falling to zero at fracture.
The steady-stage hardening plateau in (b) is lowest for the 0Cr curve (black, around the 1750–1900 MPa level on the right axis) and increases progressively for 3Cr, 6Cr and 9Cr.
No numeric data labels are printed on any curve; all reported values are read against axis gridlines.
The caption states the figure reports tensile properties of as-cast Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr: (a) engineering stress-strain curves, (b) true stress-strain and strain hardening rate curves.
The citing text states yield strength first decreases from 724 MPa to 617 MPa and then increases to 740 MPa with increasing Cr content.
The citing text states the average strain hardening rates in the steady hardening stage are 1626 MPa, 2048 MPa, 2266 MPa and 2385 MPa for the 0Cr, 3Cr, 6Cr and 9Cr alloys respectively.
The citing text states that Cr addition increases ultimate tensile strength while total elongation decreases gradually.
The citing text refers to Table 2 for the detailed tensile property values, averaged over 3 measurements; Table 2 is not part of this figure group.
